query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Brittle behavior in single‐phase high-entropy alloys emerges not from conventional intermetallic precipitation but from stress‐ and temperature‐induced chemical ordering (or nanosegregation) at grain boundaries, which reduces grain-boundary cohesion. This mechanism can be distinguished by pre-aging treatments that modify the initial grain boundary chemistry.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy with homogeneous, as-cast grain boundary composition.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled pre-aging treatment to deliberately modify the grain boundary chemical state, followed by systematic variation of strain rate and temperature during mechanical testing.
generation.conditions: Service-relevant loading conditions including intermediate temperatures (where embrittlement is observed) and high strain rates, as well as high-temperature regimes relevant to softening phenomena.
generation.mechanism: Under applied mechanical stress and specific temperature regimes, the grain boundaries of the HEA undergo stress-induced chemical segregation and local ordering. This local change in composition undermines the intergranular cohesion and leads to a transition from ductile to brittle failure, distinguishing the mechanism from conventional alloys where brittle behavior is linked to grain-boundary precipitation.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEA samples with intentionally altered grain-boundary chemistry will exhibit a measurable shift in the onset of brittle behavior (e.g., a higher or lower threshold for loss of toughness) compared to baseline as-cast samples, with detectable changes in local chemical ordering at the GBs.
generation.baseline: As-cast HEA with uniformly distributed grain boundary composition that shows a specific threshold for brittle behavior under standard loading conditions.
generation.boundary: Observed effects are expected within the range of service temperatures (including intermediate and high temperatures) and strain rates relevant to engineering applications; deviations outside these regimes might not display the predicted GB chemical ordering.
generation.uncertainty: The exact threshold conditions (strain rate, temperature) required to trigger significant chemical ordering and the precise magnitude of the toughness change remain uncertain and may vary with specific alloy composition and processing history.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one with the standard as-cast grain boundary chemistry and one with grain boundaries modified via pre-aging treatment. Subject both sets to identical mechanical testing under a range of strain rates and temperatures while simultaneously monitoring grain boundary composition via in-situ atom probe tomography and TEM.
measurements: Onset strain/stress at which embrittlement occurs.
Quantitative characterization of grain boundary chemical ordering/nanosegregation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the pre-aged samples do not exhibit any significant change in the threshold for brittle behavior or the degree of GB chemical ordering relative to the baseline, indicating that the intervention fails to alter the failure mechanism as predicted.

frame.system: An initially single‐phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy (HEA) that avoids the typical deleterious phases and microstructural evolution found in conventional alloys.
frame.goal: Develop and test a mechanistic hypothesis that explains whether and why brittle behavior (i.e. loss of toughness) emerges in these HEAs, and to contrast this mechanism with that of conventional alloys.
frame.limitation: There is currently a lack of an established, testable mechanistic understanding of toughness degradation in single-phase HEAs despite their known resistance to grain coarsening and intermetallic precipitation.
constraints: The alloy must remain compositionally complex
It must be suitable for demanding engineering service conditions
frame.regime: The hypothesis should be tested under conditions relevant to service loading boundaries, including both high-temperature (where softening can occur) and low-temperature regimes (where embrittlement is a risk).

decision.trend: Early work on HEAs focused on avoiding conventional failure modes – namely, grain‐boundary segregation and intermetallic precipitation – by designing alloys with high compositional complexity and suppressed grain coarsening (as in PMC4145285 and the successful eutectic designs). Later, studies (especially PMC6897545) found that even in single‐phase, compositionally complex HEAs, ductility loss at intermediate temperatures correlated with nanoclustering of individual principal elements at grain boundaries. This suggests that, although HEAs evade conventional brittle precipitates, they may develop a different type of chemical inhomogeneity (or stress‐induced local ordering) at GBs that undermines cohesion. Despite extended studies into dislocation behaviors and grain design, the precise conditions and kinetics by which such dynamic GB chemical ordering leads to embrittlement remain unexplained in a controlled, testable manner.
decision.unsolved: It is still unknown whether the emergence of brittleness in single‐phase HEAs is governed by stress/temperature‐induced chemical ordering or nanosegregation at grain boundaries – a mechanism distinct from the traditional precipitation seen in conventional alloys. In particular, the threshold conditions (in terms of strain rate, temperature, and prior grain boundary chemistry) that drive this transition from ductile to brittle behavior remain to be determined, and a controlled comparison that isolates this effect is lacking.
decision.lever: Systematic pre‐aging and strain rate/temperature variation to deliberately modify the grain boundary chemical state (tracked via in‑situ techniques such as atom probe tomography and TEM), comparing samples with engineered GB chemistry against a baseline HEA with as-cast GB composition.
decision.why: This approach follows the trend that HEAs, although free of deleterious intermetallics, still show loss of toughness likely due to dynamic GB nanoclustering. By controlling the grain boundary chemical state and subjecting the alloy to service-relevant loading conditions, the experiment can distinguish whether stress-induced segregation (and the resulting local ordering at GBs) is the culprit for brittle behavior. A decisive falsification would be if the modified GB chemistry, despite systematic changes in loading and temperature, does not alter the onset of brittleness compared to the baseline, thereby ruling out the nanosegregation hypothesis.
